title: Harvey Power Users: The Purposeful User — Tom Whittaker at Burges Salmon
author: Harvey Team · Tom Whittaker

dom.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value

st.t: Power users: Usage volume may obscure value
st.an: Whittaker accepts the cluster’s core distinction between access or activity and effective use, then materially develops it with an operational model: define power users by workflow fit and execution, distribute accessible specialists across teams, and use usage data diagnostically rather than as proof of value. He also broadens the framing by stressing that some needs require structural or interpersonal—not AI—solutions.
qs: But measuring [adoption](/blog/turn-ai-adoption-into-firm-wide-change) purely by prompt volume doesn’t reflect quality or outcomes.
These are the areas where we should define purpose, workflow, and data, and then identify where Harvey can augment that workflow.

st.an: Whittaker accepts the cluster’s core case for selective, context-aware deployment and workflow integration, then materially develops it with a practitioner competence framework combining legal, technical and practical judgment. His account is prescriptive rather than empirical and does not independently establish task-level gains or verification outcomes.

kp.k: Purposeful AI use matters more than usage intensity
kp.d: In this Harvey company-blog interview published April 20, 2026, Tom Whittaker argues that effective legal-AI use should serve client, colleague or case objectives rather than maximize tool usage. He defines expertise through identifying appropriate use cases, understanding workflows and executing effectively, rather than through frequency of use. These are practitioner recommendations, not quantified findings about performance.
qs: It shouldn’t be someone who simply uses a tool a lot.
One of the things we say to people is that you should use technology with purpose — you’re trying to do something better for your clients, colleagues, or case.
A power user is someone who knows how to make the best use of a product or tool, both in identifying the right use case and in understanding how it fits within a broader workflow.

kp.k: AI expertise combines law, technology, practice and collaboration
kp.d: Whittaker describes legal-AI expertise as an integrated capability: legal understanding supplies objectives and constraints, technology enables action, and practice determines implementation. He recommends developing this capability through curiosity, collaboration, real-world experience and an understanding of work across platforms and stages. Teaching colleagues is also part of his ideal power-user role.
qs: The law defines both why you’re doing something and the constraints around it. Technology is what enables it. And practice is how it actually gets done.
Ideally, you can also explain that to colleagues, teaching them and enabling them to do it themselves.
Equally important is a willingness to collaborate — to recognise what you don’t know, and to know who to involve.
Over time, you build that combined understanding of law, technology, and practice, ideally in real-world environments where you can see how things actually work and learn what delivers results.

kp.k: Distributed specialists matter more than universal power-user status
kp.d: Whittaker distinguishes everyday users from power users and rejects making everyone a power user as the adoption objective. He proposes ideally having one power user per team, with other staff knowing when to seek specialist help. His fishing analogy distinguishes teachable incremental improvements from larger opportunities that may require a specialist or small cohort; the greater long-term value of those opportunities is asserted rather than measured.
qs: A power user is different from an everyday user.
What matters is that if you’re not a power user, you know when to call on one.
But sometimes there are whales so big that you’ll always need a power user (or a small cohort) to handle them.
Catching a whale can deliver far greater, longer-term value.
Ideally, you’d have one power user per team so that when people are listening to what that sector or those clients need, they can identify where the technology could help.

kp.k: Recurring legal tasks offer workflow augmentation opportunities
kp.d: Whittaker recommends supplementing team-based expertise with a task-based approach across departments. He identifies chronologies, dramatis personae, bundle preparation and interrogation of large datasets as recurring work where the purpose, workflow and data should be defined before deciding where Harvey can augment the process. This is an augmentation recommendation, not evidence of autonomous replacement or measured productivity gains.
qs: But it should also be task-based.
There’s repeat work across departments: chronologies, dramatis personae, preparing bundles, interrogating large data sets.
These are the areas where we should define purpose, workflow, and data, and then identify where Harvey can augment that workflow.

kp.k: Adoption monitoring must look beyond frequency to outcomes
kp.d: Whittaker reports that his organization monitors overall usage, integration into practice and differences between teams, using gaps as prompts for engagement. He cautions that frequent use can fail to address the underlying problem. The interview supplies no usage figures, outcome measures or comparative study results.
qs: We look at data to understand whether usage is increasing overall and whether it’s becoming embedded in practice.
We also look at which teams are using it. If there’s a gap, that’s usually a signal to engage with those teams.
Someone could use it frequently without addressing the actual problem.

kp.k: Some problems require organizational changes rather than AI
kp.d: Whittaker argues that meeting client and colleague needs need not involve Harvey or AI, and that solutions may be structural as well as technological. His long-email example recommends discussing communication needs directly rather than automatically applying AI summarization, illustrating his broader insistence on diagnosing the problem before selecting a tool.
qs: It should be driven by purpose: are you meeting client or colleague needs and helping to achieve their objectives? Some of that isn’t Harvey, and some of it isn’t AI.
In many cases, the solution isn’t solely technological, it’s also structural.

For example, if people complain that I send long emails, the answer isn’t to summarise them with AI — it’s to pick up the phone and ask why I provided that level of detail and to make sure I understand their needs and preferences.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Tom Whittaker presents AI as a means of augmenting selected legal workflows, with value dependent on purposeful use rather than usage volume or universal expert proficiency.
pts.d: Whittaker identifies chronologies, dramatis personae, bundle preparation and interrogation of large datasets as recurring tasks where Harvey could augment workflows. He argues that effective users combine legal, technical and practical knowledge and understand client or colleague objectives. His proposed model is ideally one power user per team, with specialists or small cohorts handling more complex opportunities that can deliver greater, longer-term value. These are recommendations and qualitative claims about effective deployment, not quantified predictions of productivity, job displacement or market change. He also argues that some problems require structural or interpersonal solutions rather than AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is Whittaker’s practitioner account of adoption at Burges Salmon, supplemented by illustrative examples and analogies; no quantitative outcome evidence is supplied.
pts.d: Whittaker describes monitoring overall usage, integration into practice and differences between teams. He distinguishes those indicators from evidence of quality or successful outcomes. The document provides no usage figures, benchmark results, measured efficiency gains or specific completed matters demonstrating the claimed longer-term value. His email example illustrates why understanding needs can matter more than adding an AI tool. The interview appears on Harvey’s company blog; its promotional framing should be distinguished from Whittaker’s substantive account.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview describes current practice as of April 20, 2026 and gradual capability development, without a dated forecast.
pts.d: Whittaker conditions useful AI deployment on understanding the objective, legal and technical constraints, the broader workflow and when to involve colleagues. He anticipates that some complex tasks will continue to require specialist users or small cohorts rather than universal proficiency. The contrast between incremental improvements and greater, longer-term value is qualitative, with no specified delivery horizon. His recommendations explicitly allow for solutions that do not involve Harvey or AI.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern law-firm teams, specialist and everyday users, their colleagues and clients.
pts.d: At Burges Salmon, power users are envisaged as identifying suitable applications, integrating AI into workflows, teaching colleagues and handling complex work. Everyday users need to recognise when specialist help is appropriate rather than all becoming experts. Teams across departments may benefit from shared approaches to recurring tasks, while clients and colleagues are the intended beneficiaries of objective-led improvements. The source makes no specific claims about employment reductions, fees, legal-market shares or public access to justice.
